chapter_theme: The end of the debate with the materialist Pisasikan: Neelakesi argues that differences of karma, missing senses, memory, feelings and omens cannot come from the elements and that a soul exists; then, to the man who trusts only what he sees, she shows part of her demon form, comforts him as a mother, and he takes the Jain dharma before a marvelling court.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the materialist (பூதவாதி) who debates Neelakesi in the last sarukkam; called பிசாசகன் in 856 and பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894
the king before whose court the materialist debate is held (named in 855)
the king's court that hears the debate

875.reading: Neelakesi argues that if beings came from the elements alone, with no knowing principle, the many pups of one litter of pigs or dogs would all be alike; their differences come from deeds, as from a seed.
875.nuance: Same parents, same food, same elements, yet the litter differs: the Jain answer puts the difference in each soul's own karma. The materialist's view is given as the Jain poem states it, not in a materialist's own words. The construal of புத்தி யானின்றி (line 1) as 'without a knowing principle' is mine.

claims.claim: living beings are produced by the elements alone, with no knowing principle
the differences among the young of one litter come from their own deeds

876.reading: She presses that if an aggregate of elements can form with some elements lacking, and awareness is only the elements' own, then where the five she names are not all present the materialist must bring in a hidden element to supply the awareness.
876.nuance: A reductio: the doctrine that admits only the seen elements would need an unseen one. The verse is compressed and the steps are my reconstruction.

claims.claim: awareness is nothing but a property of the elements gathered together

877.reading: Neelakesi asks how creatures such as the crawling conch, which have earth, water and wind in their bodies and fire too since they eat, still lack the eye and the ear, if each sense were made by an element.
877.nuance: She turns the Jain grading of beings by the number of their senses against the materialist's scheme in 857, where each element yields its sense: the lower creatures have the elements but not the senses. Line 2 (ஊர் மச்சி மூக்சில) is hard to divide; 'lacking the nose' is a guess.

claims.claim: each of the five senses is made from one of the five elements
some beings, like the conch, have fewer senses though their bodies hold all the elements

878.reading: She asks what cause brings the elements together one by one in the order of awareness, and says mockingly that if they can shrink and all merge into one another she will grant that his truth stands.
878.nuance: The objection is that combination needs a cause the materialist does not name; the closing concession is ironic.

claims.claim: the elements come together of themselves to make awareness
the joining of the elements needs a cause beyond the elements

879.reading: Telling him to give up the thought that the five senses each arise from one of the five elements, Neelakesi establishes the reality of the soul that lives on.
879.nuance: The narrator's ஒட்டினாள் (line 4) reports the outcome as won: the soul's existence is set up against the materialist's reduction of sense to element in 857.

claims.claim: the five senses arise each from one of the five elements
a living soul exists

880.reading: She says that if awareness and pleasure are granted even to the one-sensed beings, the claim that they are a mere aggregate is false: wherever awareness and pleasure are, a soul is joined there.
880.nuance: ஓரறிவு (line 1) is the Jain term for the one-sensed beings, plants and the like; awareness in the lowest form of life is made the mark of a soul.

claims.claim: wherever there is awareness and pleasure, a soul is joined there

881.reading: If the body comes from wind, she argues, what work is left for the aggregate in making the soul; but if he says the soul is something apart from these five, that would be worth accepting.
881.nuance: Taking மாற்றி (line 3) as 'apart from' makes the verse an opening for the opponent to concede; the sense of line 2 is uncertain.

claims.claim: the body and its life come from wind
the soul is other than the five elements

882.reading: She calls faulty his claim that, since the five elements are real and separate and there is no soul without end or origin, everything falls apart and comes to nothing when they part.
882.nuance: This is the materialist's account of death: the elements disperse and nothing survives. Here the reply is only 'it has a fault'; the following verses give the reasons.

claims.claim: when the elements part at death all is scattered and nothing remains

883.reading: She argues that what is heard in infancy is remembered in old age, so there is a knower that never loses it, and asks who else would make men bow in worship.
883.nuance: The argument from memory: the body's elements change from childhood to old age, but what was learned stays, so the one who holds it is not the elements. Lines 3 and 4 are obscure and the second half of the reading is a guess; கீழவு (line 2) reads as கிழவு, old age.

claims.claim: memory carried from infancy to old age shows a lasting knower

884.reading: She challenges him to stand before her and insist that pain, purity, fear and dread, love, honour, deceit, courage and pleasure are made by fire.
884.nuance: The list mixes feelings with moral qualities (purity, honour, deceit): the point is that the moral life cannot be credited to an element.

claims.claim: feelings and moral qualities are not made by the material elements

885.reading: She asks whether dream, mantra, thought, the span of life, the astrology people consult and the omen of bird cries are his elements, and bids him say if he knows.
885.nuance: She counts omens, astrology and mantra as real things the elements cannot explain: the debater argues from what the world already trusts, not from Jain doctrine alone.

claims.claim: dream, mantra, thought, life-span, astrology and bird-omen are real yet are not elements

886.reading: She says the world accepts it when one reborn leads his kin to the thing he had laid away in his former life, and that though he says there is no soul in any form, the dead come back and do mischief.
886.nuance: The reborn man finding his own hidden treasure is offered as evidence outside the claimant's own mind. Line 4 (செத்து வம்மெய்திற் சில்லைமை செய்பவால்) is hard to construe; 'the dead come back' is my reading. உலகு ஒட்டும் (line 2) makes common acceptance the test.

claims.claim: one reborn can show his kin what he hid in a former life
there is no soul in any form

887.reading: She asks the man who says there are no ghosts and no rebirth why then a possessed person pinches his mouth and beats himself, and tells him to grant that a deity called by mantra, and not by trickery, comes and seizes.
887.nuance: Possession is offered as a public sign of unseen beings. The phrase அறங்கோடல் (line 4) is unclear; reading it as the deity's seizing is a guess.

claims.claim: there are no ghosts and no rebirth
a deity summoned by mantra truly comes and possesses

888.reading: When he says he will accept it, she points and bids him look, and putting aside her assumed form she shows him her power of transformation.
888.nuance: The materialist who trusts only the seen is given something to see: the demoness who has argued all the debates in a woman's form reveals what she is. விகுர்வணை (line 4) is the Jain word for this power of changing form. Line 2 (உணர்விலா முட்டை காண்கென முனகை முறுக்கியே) is obscure.
888.event: Pisasikan says he will accept the claim if shown; Neelakesi points and, dropping her assumed form, shows him her transformation.

889.reading: Knowing that even spirits and the people of the wide world weep and die at that sight, and that he would die if he saw it whole, she shows him only her mouth and her curved teeth.
889.nuance: Her restraint is the first act of care in the scene: she measures out the proof so as not to kill the man she is converting.
889.event: Neelakesi, judging that the full sight would kill him, shows Pisasikan only her mouth and curved teeth.

890.reading: He covers his eyes and falls face down; she lifts him, seats him, speaks fitting gentle words, tells him she is his friend, and calms his trembling.
890.nuance: Line 1's வழவே is unclear; the gesture sequence is plain.
890.event: Pisasikan covers his eyes and falls; Neelakesi raises him, speaks kindly as his friend, and stills his fear.

891.reading: Asked to tell what the ghost he saw was like, he says he saw its mouth, begs not to be pressed, and says he is sick with it; she tells him not to fear, that she is a mother to him, and that there is never any death.
891.nuance: என்றும் சாதலில்லை (line 4) carries the doctrinal point of the scene into comfort: what he fears ends nothing. Who says each phrase is fixed from the dialogue, and the reading of line 3's அவள் தாய் as 'a mother to you' is a guess.
891.event: Neelakesi asks Pisasikan to describe the ghost; he says he saw its mouth and is ill with fear, and she reassures him.

claims.claim: there is never death for the soul

892.reading: She tells him that the very name he bears, Pisasikan, makes him without question the ghost's son, and that if he takes the faultless dharma he is kin to her and her own, and bids him speak; and he speaks.
892.nuance: A pun: பிசாசிகன் means 'the ghost's one', so the denier of ghosts was named for them; the demoness adopts him through dharma. Taking the dharma makes him kin (சுற்றம்) of those who keep it.
892.event: Neelakesi tells Pisasikan his name makes him her son and that taking the dharma makes him her kin, and asks him to speak.

claims.claim: one who takes the faultless dharma becomes kin of those who keep it

893.reading: He says he has understood and holds firm all she told him, birth, ghosts and the rest, has taken the dharma as it should be taken, and will not forget it now.
893.nuance: The convert names first what he had denied (பிறப்பு, பேய்): the debate ends not with silence but with assent to its two disputed facts.
893.event: Pisasikan accepts rebirth and ghosts and takes the dharma.

claims.claim: rebirth and ghosts are real

894.reading: The narrator says that when Pisasikan was thus won, the king and all that royal assembly marvelled, and all the people honoured the woman of searching learning as their lady.
894.nuance: This closes the last debate of the work. பேந்தரு தோற்றம் (line 1) is obscure; it may describe the fear-struck look of the converted man.
894.event: The king and his assembly marvel at Pisasikan's conversion, and all honour Neelakesi.

links.note: In 857 the materialist says the five elements become eye, nose, tongue, body and ear with their five objects; in 879 Neelakesi tells him to give up that very thought and sets up the soul.
links.teaches: The materialist's derivation of each sense from an element is the exact point Neelakesi chooses to deny, so the soul she proves is defined against a sense apparatus made of matter.

links.note: In 49 the sage knows she may try to frighten him with her transformations (விகுர்வணை) and fail; in 888 she uses the same power of transformation to frighten the materialist into belief.
links.teaches: The demon's power to change shape, useless against the Jain sage at the start, becomes at the end the Jain debater's proof of unseen beings, so the same faculty passes from assault to teaching.

links.note: In 134 Neelakesi likens the sage to a mother who nurses her infant even when it hurts her, and drops her false form; in 891 and 892 she, the demoness, calls herself a mother to the frightened Pisasikan and makes him kin through dharma.
links.teaches: The work closes its debates by repeating its opening conversion one step down: the demoness who was mothered into dharma now mothers a man into it, so conversion is shown as a lineage passed on.

links.note: In 7 the poet asks readers not to scorn his work, since people take even a bird's cry as meaningful; in 885 Neelakesi counts the omen of bird cries among the things the elements cannot explain.
links.teaches: The poem leans twice on the common trust in bird-omens, once to defend itself and once to defeat the materialist, which shows how much of its case rests on what the world already accepts.

links.note: Both epics answer a materialist who accepts only perception: Manimekalai shows him that he knows his own parents only by inference; Neelakesi grants his rule and gives him a perception, the sight of a ghost.
links.teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain epic meet the same Lokayata rule in opposite ways: one turns the rule against itself and leaves the materialist answered, the other satisfies the rule and leaves him converted.

links.note: Manimekalai asks whether some have not known a former birth, and the materialist dismisses such knowledge as the delusion of the god-struck or the dreamer; Neelakesi offers the reborn man who leads his kin to the treasure he hid.
links.teaches: The reborn man's found treasure is a check outside his own mind, so it meets the very objection the materialist raised against Manimekalai's appeal to remembered births.

links.note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to exist will be set down on earth as a demon; the materialist who denies ghosts is named Pisasikan, the ghost's one, and the demoness claims him as son once he takes the dharma.
links.teaches: The epic plays the couplet's sentence out and reverses its sting: the denier is indeed reckoned of the demons, but as their adopted kin through dharma rather than as an object of scorn.

gains.a: Neelakesi's pun on the name gains a known moral frame, the denier of common belief as a demon among men.
gains.b: The Kural's unnamed 'what the world holds' gets a content, ghosts and rebirth, and a case where the denier is won back rather than condemned.

links.note: Neelakesi asks what cause brings the elements together, since they cannot join themselves; Tirumular sets unknowing maya beside the knowing soul and calls the making of elements and senses the fivefold work of grace.
links.teaches: Both texts deny that unknowing matter assembles itself into a knower, but where the Jain debater leaves the cause in the soul and its deeds, the Saiva verse gives it to grace.

gains.a: Neelakesi's open question gains the answer a rival theist school gives, showing which answer the Jain debater leaves unsaid.
gains.b: Tirumular's assignment of elements and senses to grace gains the opponent it presupposes: the materialist for whom the elements need no cause at all.

links.note: The materialist says that when the elements part, all comes to nothing; the Siddhar says he saw the five elements die and fall and the five senses burn and fall.
links.teaches: The Siddhar describes as his own experience the parting of elements and senses that the materialist says must end awareness, and he remains to report it, which is the case Neelakesi argues for and does not show.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare rejection gains a first-person witness who outlasts the falling away of the elements.
gains.b: The Siddhar's vision gains its doctrinal stake: it is the very event the materialist claims would leave no one to see it.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (பூத வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008

new_concepts.gloss: a sense faculty; in Jain teaching beings are graded by how many of the five senses they have
new_concepts.label_source: as declared in neelakesi ch004; here the verses speak of the senses as இந்தியங்கள் (879) and of the one-sensed (ஓரறிவு, 880)

new_concepts.gloss: the materialist doctrine that the elements alone make up the world and that awareness arises from their combination
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (பூத வாதச் சருக்கம்) and the opponent's title பூதவாதி (854)

source_issues: 877 line 3 was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தேரி); line 2 (ஊர் மச்சி மூக்சில) has an unclear word division.
875 line 1 (புத்தி யானின்றி) is hard to divide.
883 line 2 has கீழவு where கிழவு (old age) seems meant; lines 3 and 4 are obscure.
886 line 3 reads இல்லுயு ரென்றி, apparently for இல் உயிர் என்றி.
888 line 2 (உணர்விலா முட்டை காண்கென முனகை முறுக்கியே) is obscure and may be corrupt.
890 line 1 has a stray space in கண் புதைத்துக் and an unclear வழவே.
The opponent is spelt பிசாசகன் in 856 and பிசாசிகன் in 892 and 894.
